questions.question: What is the key difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?
questions.title: Interface vs Abstract Class — Core Differences
questions.direct_answer: An **interface** defines a pure contract — no state (fields), supports multiple implementation, all methods are public. An **abstract class** can have state (instance fields), constructors, protected methods, and supports single inheritance. Use interface for capabilities/contracts; abstract class for partial shared implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to clearly articulate the design differences and when to choose each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying interfaces are always better or that abstract classes are obsolete — both have distinct use cases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give real Java examples: Runnable/Comparable as interfaces (capabilities), AbstractList/HttpServlet as abstract classes (partial implementations)

sections.title: Contract vs Partial Implementation
Interface vs Abstract Class Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | Interface | Abstract Class |
|---|---|---|
| State (instance fields) | No (only static final constants) | Yes |
| Constructor | No | Yes |
| Inheritance | Multiple (implements many) | Single (extends one) |
| Method access | All public | public, protected, package |
| Concrete methods | default/static only (Java 8+) | Full concrete methods |
| When to use | Capability/contract (Runnable, Comparable) | Partial implementation with shared state |
| Instantiation | No | No |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The fundamental difference is that an interface defines a pure contract — no state, no constructors, multiple implementation allowed. An abstract class is more like an incomplete class — it can have instance fields, constructors, protected methods, and concrete logic, but only single inheritance. The decision rule I use: interface for capabilities that many unrelated classes should have — like Runnable or Comparable. Abstract class when you have shared state or partial implementation — like AbstractList or HttpServlet where many subclasses share the same base logic.

questions.question: Can an interface have instance variables in Java?
questions.title: Instance Variables in Java Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: No. All variables declared in an interface are implicitly `public static final` — they are **constants**, not instance variables. You cannot have mutable instance state in an interface. This is because interfaces define contracts without implementation, and instance state would require object construction which interfaces don't support.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness that interface variables are constants and understanding why
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Declaring a variable in an interface thinking it's an instance field — it's a static final constant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that since interfaces have no constructors and can't be instantiated, there's no mechanism for per-object state

sections.title: Interface Variables Are Always Constants
Key Points
sections.content:
- Interface variables are implicitly `public static final` — constants
- You must initialize them at declaration (since they're final)
- No instance variables allowed in interfaces
- Constants are accessed via the interface name: `Config.MAX_SIZE`
- Implementing class inherits the constant — can access without qualification
- This is a common source of accidental constants: developers declare 'fields' in interfaces expecting instance state
- Abstract classes CAN have mutable instance fields — this is a key differentiator

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: No, interfaces cannot have instance variables. Any variable you declare in an interface is automatically treated as public static final — a constant. You can't change it, and it belongs to the interface itself, not to any object. The reason is that interfaces can't be instantiated, so there's no object to own instance state. If I write `int count = 0` inside an interface, it becomes a public constant, not a mutable field. For mutable instance state, you need a class — abstract or concrete.

questions.question: Why can a class implement multiple interfaces but only extend one class in Java?
questions.title: Multiple Interface Implementation vs Single Class Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: A class can implement multiple interfaces because interfaces have no state and pre-Java-8 had no method bodies — so there's no **implementation conflict** (diamond problem). Classes can only extend one class to avoid ambiguity when two parent classes have different implementations of the same method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the diamond problem and why multiple interface implementation is safe
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being able to articulate why multiple interfaces are safe but multiple classes are not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java 8 default methods reintroduce a version of the problem for interfaces, and how Java resolves it

sections.title: Why Multiple Interfaces Are Safe (Usually)
Key Points
sections.content:
- Multiple interface implementation: safe pre-Java-8 because interfaces had no implementation
- Single class inheritance: prevents diamond problem (ambiguous inherited implementation)
- Java 8 default methods: can cause conflict between interfaces — resolved by mandatory override
- A class can both `extend` one class AND `implement` multiple interfaces
- Interfaces give 'multiple inheritance of type' without 'multiple inheritance of implementation'
- The JVM can know with certainty which method to call when there's only one implementation source

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A class can implement multiple interfaces because, before Java 8, interfaces had no method implementations — they were pure contracts. If Duck implements Flyable and Swimmable, Duck itself provides all the implementations, so there's no ambiguity. With single class inheritance, the diamond problem occurs: if D extends both B and C, and they both override a method from A differently, the JVM can't decide which to use. Java solves this by allowing only one parent class. Java 8 default methods bring a version of this to interfaces too, but Java handles it by requiring the implementing class to explicitly override any conflicting default method.

questions.question: When should you use an interface versus an abstract class in Java?
questions.title: Choosing Between Interface and Abstract Class in Java
questions.direct_answer: Use an **interface** when defining a **capability or contract** that unrelated classes should share (`Runnable`, `Comparable`, `Serializable`). Use an **abstract class** when you have **shared state and partial implementation** that related classes should inherit — like `AbstractList`, `HttpServlet`, or a base `Vehicle` class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical design judgment — not just knowing the differences but knowing when to apply each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always defaulting to interface or always defaulting to abstract class without justification
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the 'IS-A vs CAN-DO' heuristic: abstract class for IS-A (Dog IS-A Animal), interface for CAN-DO (Duck CAN-DO Flyable)

sections.title: The Design Decision Framework
sections.content:
Here's the mental model: **abstract class = IS-A relationship with shared code**, **interface = CAN-DO capability**.

**Use interface when:**
- Unrelated classes need the same capability: `Thread` and `Timer` both implement `Runnable` — they're not related but both CAN run tasks
- You want multiple implementation: a class can be `Runnable AND Comparable AND Serializable`
- You're defining an API contract: `PaymentService`, `EmailSender`, `Logger`

**Use abstract class when:**
- Classes share IS-A relationship AND common state/code:
```java
abstract class HttpServlet {           // Abstract class
    protected HttpSession session;     // shared state
    final void service(req, resp) {   // shared algorithm
        String method = req.getMethod();
        if ("GET".equals(method)) doGet(req, resp);
        else doPost(req, resp);
    }
    abstract void doGet(req, resp);   // subclass fills in
    abstract void doPost(req, resp);
}
```
- You need constructors, protected methods, or non-public access
- The Template Method pattern applies

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Interface: unrelated types sharing a capability (CAN-DO), multiple implementation needed
- Abstract class: closely related types sharing state and partial logic (IS-A), single inheritance OK
- Real Java examples — Interface: `Runnable`, `Comparable`, `Iterable`, `Serializable`
- Real Java examples — Abstract class: `AbstractList`, `HttpServlet`, `AbstractController`
- Modern advice: default to interface first; switch to abstract class only when you need state or constructors
- Interfaces give flexibility — you can always add an abstract class on top that implements the interface
- Abstract class couples subclasses to its implementation; interface is more loosely coupled

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: My decision rule is: use interface for capabilities or contracts that unrelated classes should share — like Runnable, Comparable, or Serializable. A Thread and a Timer are completely unrelated classes, but both can implement Runnable. Use abstract class when you have closely related classes that share actual state and partial implementation — like HttpServlet which has shared fields and a concrete service() method with abstract doGet() and doPost() that subclasses fill in. In modern Java, I'd default to interface first, and only use abstract class when I specifically need instance fields, constructors, or protected methods.

questions.question: Can an interface extend another interface in Java?
questions.title: Interface Extending Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: Yes. An interface can `extend` one or more other interfaces using the `extends` keyword. The extending interface **inherits all abstract methods** of the parent interface(s) and can add new ones. A class implementing the child interface must implement all inherited abstract methods.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of interface inheritance and that interfaces (unlike classes) CAN extend multiple interfaces
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking interfaces can only be implemented by classes — they can also be extended by other interfaces
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the real Java example: List extends Collection extends Iterable — a hierarchy of interfaces

sections.title: Interface Inheritance — Extending Contracts
Key Points
sections.content:
- Interface uses `extends` (not `implements`) to inherit from another interface
- Interfaces CAN extend multiple interfaces: `interface C extends A, B`
- All abstract methods from parent interfaces are inherited
- A class implementing the child interface must implement all inherited abstract methods
- Default methods are also inherited and can be overridden
- Real Java example: `List extends Collection extends Iterable` — 3-level hierarchy
- Unlike class inheritance, there's no diamond ambiguity issue for abstract methods

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Yes, an interface can extend another interface using the `extends` keyword — and unlike classes, an interface can extend multiple interfaces at once. The child interface inherits all abstract methods from the parent interfaces and can add its own. Any class that implements the child interface must implement all the inherited abstract methods from the entire hierarchy. The Java standard library does this a lot — `List extends Collection`, which extends `Iterable`. A class implementing `List` must implement methods from all three.

questions.question: What is a marker interface in Java and what are some examples?
questions.title: Marker Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **marker interface** is an empty interface with no methods or fields. Its sole purpose is to **mark or tag** a class to signal metadata to the JVM or frameworks. Examples: `Serializable` (marks class for serialization), `Cloneable` (enables `Object.clone()`), `Remote` (marks RMI remote objects).

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of marker interfaces and their purpose — metadata signaling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying marker interfaces are useless because they have no methods — they serve an important signaling purpose
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that annotations (since Java 5) are the modern preferred alternative to marker interfaces, and give an example

sections.title: Empty Interface as a Tag
Key Points
sections.content:
- Marker interface: empty interface used to tag/mark a class for special treatment
- Three classic examples: `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, `Remote`
- How it works: the JVM or framework checks `obj instanceof MarkerInterface`
- `Cloneable` without `Object.clone()` has no effect — must override `clone()` too
- Modern replacement: annotations (since Java 5) — `@Override`, `@Deprecated`, custom annotations
- Annotations are preferred: can carry data, more expressive, checked by annotation processors
- Marker interfaces still exist for legacy reasons and JVM-level integration

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A marker interface is an empty interface — no methods, no fields. Its purpose is purely to tag a class so the JVM or a framework can detect it using instanceof. The classic example is `Serializable` — if a class implements it, `ObjectOutputStream` knows it can serialize it. If not, it throws an exception. `Cloneable` works similarly for the clone() method. In modern Java, annotations are the preferred alternative to marker interfaces because they're more expressive and can carry additional data. But marker interfaces are still around for legacy and JVM-level reasons.
